lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5, what would a real bank never ask for in a message? (Your password.) Today: how to spot a scam, and what to do about one.

A scam is a trick to take your money, your things or your personal details. Scammers use messages, emails, texts, pop-ups and game chats. They may pretend to be a bank, a shop, a game or even a friend.

Warning signs: a prize you never entered for; a rush ('act now or lose it'); a request for your password, PIN or card details; a link with an odd spelling; a request to keep it secret; something too good to be true.
Game scams: 'free gold makers', and people who offer to double your items if you hand them over first. Fake login pages look like the real game. A game never needs your password to give you anything.

picture.subject: You WON 10,000 free gold!!
lines: Just type your game password below.

lesson.text: Stop, think, check: don't click the link or reply. Check by going to the real website or app yourself, not through the message. Ask: who sent this, and how would they know me?
Tell a trusted grown-up at once, even if you already clicked or shared something: it is never too late, and you are not in trouble. Use REPORT and BLOCK in the game, and change a password you shared.
Protect yourself: use a strong, different password for each account. Keep your passwords secret from everyone but your grown-up, and turn on the extra login check when you can.
Try it in the world: put up a Scam Spotter sign in your village with the warning signs. Then act out a scam message with a friend, and practise the safe reply. Next: sustainable choices.

exercises.hint: Scammers pretend to be someone else.
choices: a trick to take money or details
exercises.explain: A trick to take your money, things or personal details.

exercises.prompt: A real game will never ask for your password to give you a prize.
exercises.explain: True: a game never needs your password to give you anything.

exercises.prompt: Which is a warning sign of a scam?
exercises.hint: Can you win something you never entered?
choices: a prize you never entered for
exercises.explain: A prize you never entered for is too good to be true.

exercises.prompt: A message says 'Act now or lose your account!' What is this trick?
exercises.hint: Why would a scammer want you to act fast?
choices: rushing you so you don't think
exercises.explain: Scammers rush you so you act before you stop and think.

exercises.prompt: Who should you tell if you get a scam message?
exercises.hint: It is never too late to get help.
exercises.explain: A trusted grown-up, and use REPORT in the game.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a scam's warning sign, or a safe thing to do?
items: asks you to keep it secret
a link with an odd spelling
exercises.hint: Scams rush, tempt and ask for secrets; safe habits slow down and get help.
exercises.explain: Warning signs: secrets, odd links, doubling offers. Safe: typing the address yourself, telling a grown-up.

exercises.prompt: Someone offers to double your gold if you give it to them first. What should you do?
exercises.hint: What happens once you hand it over?
choices: say no, block and report them
exercises.explain: It is a scam: say no, block and report them.

exercises.prompt: If you have already clicked a scam link, it is too late to tell anyone.
exercises.explain: False: tell a trusted grown-up at once; it is never too late, and you are not in trouble.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: tells the game about a problem
a secret key for an account
exercises.explain: Phishing: fishing for details. Password: a secret key. Pop-up: a sudden window. REPORT: tells the game.

exercises.prompt: How should you check a message that says it is from your bank?
exercises.hint: Do not use anything the message gives you.
choices: go to the real app or website yourself
exercises.explain: Go to the real app or website yourself, with a grown-up.

exercises.prompt: A 'friend' on a new number asks for gold urgently and says 'tell no one'. Which signs show a scam?
exercises.hint: Look for the warning signs from the lesson.
choices: a new number, a rush and a secret
exercises.explain: A new number, a rush and a request for secrecy are all warning signs.

exercises.prompt: A scam promises to turn 50 gold into 500 gold in one day. How many times bigger is that promise?
exercises.hint: Divide the promised amount by what you put in.
exercises.explain: 500 ÷ 50 = 10 times: far too good to be true.

exercises.prompt: Why should each account have a different password?
exercises.hint: What if a scammer learned one password?
choices: if one leaks, the others stay safe
exercises.explain: If one password leaks, the others still protect your other accounts.

exercises.prompt: A pop-up says your device has a virus and asks you to call a number. What is best?
exercises.hint: Who made the pop-up, and why the rush?
choices: close it and tell a grown-up
exercises.explain: It is a common scam: close it and tell a grown-up.

exercises.prompt: A website with a padlock sign is always safe.
exercises.hint: What does the padlock really show?
exercises.explain: False: the padlock only means the connection is private; scam websites can have one too.

exercises.prompt: Sort the messages: probably a scam, or probably fine?
items: You won a prize! Send your password.
Double your gold: send it to me first!
Act now or lose your account!
exercises.hint: Look for the warning signs: prizes, rushing, passwords, secrets, things too good to be true.
exercises.explain: Scams: a prize that wants your password, an offer to double your gold, and 'act now or lose your account'. Fine: an expected note from your teacher, and Mum about tea.

exercises.prompt: You clicked a strange link and typed your password. Order what to do.
items: Change that password with your grown-up.
Tell a trusted grown-up at once.
exercises.hint: First stop, then get help, then fix what was shared.
exercises.explain: Stop and type nothing more, tell a trusted grown-up at once (you are not in trouble), then change that password together.

exercises.prompt: Match each scam message to its warning sign.
exercises.hint: Each message shows one of the signs on cards 2 and 3.
exercises.explain: A free gold maker that wants you to log in is a fake login page. 'Tell no one' asks for secrecy. A prize you never entered for is too good to be true. 'Only 5 minutes left!' rushes you.
